blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 3 (Chemical Bonding), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 Define chemical bond. Name the types of bonds included in this term.
blocks.explanation: A chemical bond is the force that holds together two or more atoms, molecules or ions. The term includes ionic, covalent, dative and metallic bonds, as well as intermolecular (van der Waals) forces.

book_ref.quote: A chemical bond is the force that holds together two or more atoms, molecules or ions.

blocks.prompt: 2 Why are van der Waals forces usually not termed pure chemical bonds?
blocks.explanation: Because they are weak. They act between molecules and do not form new species, while true chemical bonds are much stronger.

book_ref.quote: However, being weak enough, van der Waals forces are usually not termed as pure chemical bonds.

blocks.prompt: 3 State the Lewis concept of bonding.
blocks.explanation: According to Lewis, atoms make bonds to complete their outermost shells and attain a noble gas-like configuration. This is mostly attained by forming an octet in the valence shell.

book_ref.quote: Lewis concept of bonding gives a simple explanation of the formation of all types of bonds.

blocks.prompt: 4 What is an ionic bond? Explain its formation in NaCl briefly.
blocks.explanation: An ionic bond forms by complete transfer of electrons from an atom of low ionization energy to an atom of high electron affinity. Na (2, 8, 1) loses one electron to give Na⁺ (2, 8); Cl (2, 8, 7) gains it to give Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8). The oppositely charged ions are held by a strong ionic bond in the NaCl crystal.

book_ref.quote: the ionic bond is formed by the complete transfer of electrons from an atom with low ionization energy

blocks.prompt: 5 Between which groups of elements are ionic bonds expected? Why?
blocks.explanation: Between group 1 and 2 metals and group 16 and 17 elements. The metals have low ionization energy and lose electrons easily; the group 16 and 17 elements have high electron affinity and gain them.

book_ref.quote: A similar type of bond is expected between group 1 and 2 metals and groups 16 and 17 elements.

blocks.prompt: 6 Define covalent bond. How does Cl₂ attain stability?
blocks.explanation: A covalent bond is formed by mutual sharing of electrons between two atoms. In Cl₂ each Cl atom shares one electron; each completes its valence shell (octet) and attains the nearest noble gas configuration.

book_ref.quote: While sharing electrons, each atom completes its valence shell and attains the nearest noble gas configuration.

blocks.prompt: 7 Why is the bond in Cl₂ non-polar while the bond in HCl is polar?
blocks.explanation: In Cl₂ both atoms have exactly the same electronegativity, so the shared pair is shared equally and no atom carries a charge. In HCl, Cl is more electronegative, so the electron density shifts towards Cl, making the bond polar.

book_ref.quote: The electronegativity of the two atoms is exactly the same

blocks.prompt: 8 Differentiate between non-polar and polar covalent bonds.
blocks.explanation: A non-polar bond is between atoms of equal electronegativity; a polar bond is between atoms of different electronegativity.

book_ref.quote: A covalent bond may be non-polar or polar in character.

rows: Formed between atoms of the same electronegativity.
Formed between atoms of different electronegativity.
Bonded atoms remain electrically neutral.
One atom carries δ⁺ and the other δ⁻.
Examples: H₂, Cl₂, F₂, Br₂, I₂.
Examples: H–Cl, H–Br, H₂O.

blocks.text: Dative bond (coordinate covalent bond), printed as 3.13

blocks.prompt: 9 Define dative bond. Name the donor and acceptor in the formation of the hydronium ion.
blocks.explanation: A dative (coordinate covalent) bond forms between two atoms when the shared pair of electrons is donated by one of the bonding atoms. In H₃O⁺ the oxygen of H₂O (with two lone pairs) is the donor and the electron-deficient proton H⁺ is the acceptor: H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺.

book_ref.quote: A dative bond is formed between two atoms when the shared pair of electrons is donated by one of the bonding atoms.

blocks.prompt: 10 Why does carbon monoxide contain a dative bond?
blocks.explanation: Oxygen and carbon first form a normal double covalent bond, but carbon's octet is still incomplete; it needs one more pair. Oxygen donates one of its lone pairs to carbon, forming a dative bond.

book_ref.quote: However, the valency of carbon is not satisfied with these bonds.

blocks.prompt: 11 How is a coordinate covalent bond formed in ozone? Which atoms carry charges?
blocks.explanation: Ozone forms from O₂ and a free oxygen atom (O). One oxygen of O₂ donates a lone pair to the free O atom, making a coordinate bond. The central O (double bond on one side, coordinate bond on the other) carries a positive charge; the accepting O carries a negative charge.

book_ref.quote: It is formed by a reaction between the oxygen molecule with an oxygen atom

blocks.prompt: 12 What are polyatomic ions? Give two examples with correct charges.
blocks.explanation: Polyatomic ions are ions composed of more than one type of atom; their net charge is their formal charge. Except NH₄⁺ they mostly carry a negative charge, e.g. carbonate CO₃²⁻ and nitrate NO₃⁻.

book_ref.quote: Polyatomic ions are the ions composed of more than one type of atoms.

blocks.prompt: 13 What is meant by an expanded octet? Give two examples.
blocks.explanation: In some polyatomic ions the central atom violates the octet rule by expanding its electron density to higher (d) orbitals and holds more than eight valence electrons. Examples: SO₄²⁻, ClO₄⁻, PO₄³⁻.

book_ref.quote: These are said to have expanded octets.

blocks.prompt: 14 Show that S in SO₄²⁻ exceeds the octet by 4 electrons.
blocks.explanation: In the Lewis structure S has two double bonds and two single bonds. Valence electrons = 2(4) + 2(2) = 12. 12 − 8 = 4, so S exceeds the octet by 4 electrons.

book_ref.quote: From the Lewis structures of SO₄²⁻, we can calculate the number of electrons around the central S atom.

blocks.prompt: 15 How do d orbitals allow sulfur to form more bonds than its ground state suggests?
blocks.explanation: Ground-state S has two unpaired 3p electrons. Moving one 3p electron into 3d gives four unpaired electrons (3s² 3p³ 3d¹, as in SO₂); also promoting one 3s electron gives six (3s¹ 3p³ 3d², the state for six bonds in SO₄²⁻). This explains the variable oxidation states of S.

book_ref.quote: The presence of d-orbital allows this configuration to extend to 4 unpaired electrons

blocks.prompt: 16 Calculate the number of electrons around the central iodine in I₃⁻.
blocks.explanation: Central I has 2 single bonds and 3 lone pairs. Electrons = 2(2) + 2(3) = 4 + 6 = 10. So the octet expands by 2 electrons.

book_ref.quote: In the same way, we can calculate the number of valence electrons around the central iodine atom in the tri-iodide ion.

blocks.prompt: 17 Using the chapter's counting method, find the number of electrons around Xe in XeF₄.
blocks.explanation: Xe has 4 single bonds and 2 lone pairs. Electrons = 2(4) + 2(2) = 8 + 4 = 12, i.e. 4 more than an octet (expanded octet).

book_ref.quote: XeF₄ is an AB₆ type molecule with four bond pairs and two lone pairs.

blocks.text: 3.2 Electronegativity and the type of bond

blocks.prompt: 18 How does electronegativity difference decide the type of bond?
blocks.explanation: Difference less than 0.4: pure (non-polar) covalent bond; between 0.4 and 1.8: polar covalent bond; above 1.8: ionic bond. The larger the difference, the more polar the bond.

book_ref.quote: The difference in electronegativity of two bonded atoms provides an approximate measure of the bond polarity

blocks.prompt: 19 Electronegativities Mg = 1.2 and O = 3.5 (given). Predict the type of bond in MgO.
blocks.explanation: Difference = 3.5 − 1.2 = 2.3. This is above 1.8, so the bond in MgO is ionic.

book_ref.quote: This is why H-H bond is purely non-polar, H-Cl a polar covalent bond, whereas NaCl is an ionic compound.

blocks.prompt: 20 Electronegativities H = 2.1, O = 3.5 and Br = 2.8 (given). Which bond is more polar, O–H or H–Br?
blocks.explanation: O–H: 3.5 − 2.1 = 1.4; H–Br: 2.8 − 2.1 = 0.7. Both are polar covalent (0.4-1.8), but O–H, with the larger difference, is more polar.

book_ref.quote: When it is large, the bond is polar covalent or ionic.

blocks.text: Dipole moment and polarity of molecules

blocks.prompt: 21 What does the dipole moment of a molecule measure? What does a higher value indicate?
blocks.explanation: Dipole moment is a quantitative measurement of the polarity of a bond or a molecule (a dipole has δ⁺ on one part and δ⁻ on the other). It is measured in Debye (D); a higher dipole moment indicates higher polarity.

book_ref.quote: It is a quantitative measurement of the polarity of a bond or a molecule.

blocks.prompt: 22 Why does HF have partial charges on its atoms? Which way is its dipole moment directed?
blocks.explanation: H and F are different elements, so the electron distribution is uneven: F (more electronegative) gets δ⁻ and H gets δ⁺. The dipole moment is directed from the positive end to the negative end, i.e. from H to F.

book_ref.quote: In compounds such as HF, where the bonded atoms are from different elements

blocks.prompt: 23 How does the dipole moment of water prove that it is not linear?
blocks.explanation: A linear H–O–H would have zero dipole moment, as the two bond moments would cancel. Water has a dipole moment of 1.85 D, so its bond moments do not cancel: water is non-linear (v-shaped).

book_ref.quote: The non-zero dipole moment value shows that water is a non-linear molecule.

blocks.prompt: 24 BeCl₂ has polar bonds but zero dipole moment. Explain.
blocks.explanation: BeCl₂ is linear with two identical Cl atoms at 180° on both sides of Be. The two Be–Cl bond moments are equal in amount and opposite in direction, so they cancel: net dipole moment is zero.

book_ref.quote: The individual Be-Cl bond moments are cancelled out as they are opposite in direction and equal in amount.

blocks.prompt: 25 Is SO₂ polar? What does its dipole moment show about its shape?
blocks.explanation: Yes. SO₂ has a dipole moment of 1.61 D (opposite in direction to that of water). A non-zero dipole moment shows the S=O bond moments do not cancel, so SO₂ is angular (v-shaped), not linear.

book_ref.quote: In contrast, SO₂ has a dipole moment of 1.61 D and in opposite direction to that in water.

blocks.prompt: 26 Differentiate between polar and non-polar molecules with examples.
blocks.explanation: Polar molecules have a net dipole moment; non-polar molecules have zero net dipole moment.

book_ref.quote: Higher dipole moment indicates high polarity in a molecule.

rows: Have a net dipole moment.
Net dipole moment is zero.
Bond moments do not cancel (unsymmetrical, e.g. bent shape).
Bond moments cancel because of a symmetrical structure.
Examples: HF, H₂O (1.85 D), SO₂ (1.61 D), H₂S.
Examples: BeCl₂, BF₃, CCl₄.

blocks.text: 3.3.2 Valence shell electron pair repulsion model (VSEPR)

blocks.prompt: 27 What is the basic assumption of the VSEPR model?
blocks.explanation: A molecule takes a shape in which the repulsions among the valence electron pairs of the central atom are minimum. For this the electron pairs arrange themselves as far apart as possible, and this arrangement decides the geometry.

book_ref.quote: It is based on the assumption that a molecule will take a shape such that the electronic repulsions

blocks.prompt: 28 Why do lone pairs exert greater repulsion than bond pairs?
blocks.explanation: A lone pair is held by a single nucleus, while a bond pair is shared by two nuclei. So lone pairs occupy more space and push (compress) the bond pairs. Order: lp-lp > lp-bp > bp-bp.

book_ref.quote: As a result, the non-bonding electron pairs exert greater repulsive forces on bonding electron pairs

blocks.prompt: 29 Differentiate between electron pair geometry and the shape of a molecule.
blocks.explanation: Electron pair geometry counts all pairs; the shape counts only the atoms.

book_ref.quote: The electron pair geometry of a molecule is determined by the total number of electron pairs around

rows: Decided by the total number of electron pairs (bond pairs + lone pairs) around the central atom.
Decided by the positions of the atoms only, excluding lone pairs.
NH₃: tetrahedral.
NH₃: pyramidal.
H₂O: tetrahedral.
H₂O: angular (v-shaped).

blocks.prompt: 30 Give the steps used to predict the shape of a molecule by the VSEPR model.
blocks.explanation: (1) Choose the central atom: the least electronegative atom or the element with the fewest atoms (C in CCl₄). (2) Count all electron pairs (bond pairs + lone pairs) around it. (3) The total pairs give the electron pair geometry. (4) Find the actual shape, excluding the lone pairs.

book_ref.quote: The following steps are followed to predict the shape of a molecule.

blocks.prompt: 31 How are multiple bonds treated in the VSEPR model? Give an example.
blocks.explanation: The two pairs of a double bond (or three of a triple bond) have higher charge density but are counted as a single pair. So SO₃, with three S=O bonds, counts as three pairs and is perfectly trigonal (120°).

book_ref.quote: The two electron pairs of a double bond and three electron pairs of a triple bond

blocks.prompt: 32 Why is SnCl₂ v-shaped although it has three electron pairs around Sn?
blocks.explanation: Sn has 4 outer electrons; it makes two bonds with Cl and keeps the other two as a lone pair. The lone pair occupies one corner of the triangle, so excluding it the shape is v-shaped with angle less than 120°.

book_ref.quote: One of the corners of the triangle is occupied by this lone pair

blocks.prompt: 33 Why is the bond angle of NH₃ 107° instead of 109.5°?
blocks.explanation: NH₃ has three bond pairs and one lone pair around N (AB₄ type). The lone pair repels the bond pairs more strongly (lp-bp > bp-bp) and compresses them, so the angle falls from 109.5° to 107° and the shape becomes triangular pyramidal.

book_ref.quote: This effect compels ammonia to assume a triangular pyramidal shape with reduced bond angles

blocks.prompt: 34 Why is the bond angle of NF₃ (102.5°) smaller than that of NH₃ (107°)?
blocks.explanation: (i) Strongly polar N–F bonds make N pull the lone pair closer to its nucleus, so the lone pair repels the bond pairs more strongly. (ii) The N–F bond pairs lie closer to F than to N; their greater distance weakens their mutual repulsion, so the bonds come closer.

book_ref.quote: The first reason being the strong polarity of N-F bond, due to which N atom pulls the lone pair closer to its nucleus.

blocks.prompt: 35 Explain why H₂O is v-shaped with a bond angle of 104.5°.
blocks.explanation: H₂O has four electron pairs (tetrahedral geometry): two corners hold lone pairs and two hold bond pairs. Excluding the lone pairs the shape is angular (v-shaped). The greater repulsion of the two lone pairs reduces the angle to 104.5°.

book_ref.quote: Two of the corners of the tetrahedron are occupied by two lone pairs and the remaining two by bond pairs.

blocks.prompt: 36 Compare the shapes of H₃O⁺ and NH₂⁻ using VSEPR.
blocks.explanation: Both are AB₄ type with tetrahedral electron pair geometry, but their lone pairs differ.

book_ref.quote: The hydronium ion [H₃O]⁺ is formed when a water molecule captures a proton.

rows: Three bond pairs and one lone pair on O.
Two bond pairs and two lone pairs on N.
Trigonal pyramidal, like NH₃.
Bent (v-shaped), like H₂O.

blocks.prompt: 37 Describe the positions of atoms in the trigonal bipyramidal PCl₅ molecule.
blocks.explanation: Three Cl atoms lie at the corners of a planar triangle (angles 120°), and two lie on an axis perpendicular to the plane, one above and one below. The angle between an axial and a planar atom is 90°.

book_ref.quote: In a trigonal bipyramid, three positions lie along the corners of the planar triangle

blocks.prompt: 38 Why is the tri-iodide ion linear although it is an AB₅ system?
blocks.explanation: The central I has five electron pairs: two bond pairs and three lone pairs, so the electron pair geometry is trigonal bipyramidal. The three lone pairs occupy the trigonal plane and the two I atoms sit on the axis above and below it, so excluding lone pairs the shape is linear (180°).

book_ref.quote: Tri-iodide ion [I₃]⁻ is linear, although it is an AB₅ system.

blocks.prompt: 39 Differentiate between the shapes of SF₆ and XeF₄.
blocks.explanation: Both have six electron pairs (AB₆, octahedral geometry), but XeF₄ has two lone pairs.

book_ref.quote: In this geometry, four electron pairs are at the corners of a planar square

rows: Six bond pairs, no lone pair.
Four bond pairs and two lone pairs (at 180°).
Shape octahedral.
Shape square planar.
All F–S–F angles 90°.
All F–Xe–F angles 90°.

blocks.prompt: 40 How many corners, faces, edges and bond angles does a tetrahedral shape have?
blocks.explanation: A tetrahedron has four corners, four faces, six edges and six bond angles, ideally of 109.5° each.

book_ref.quote: The tetrahedral shape has four corners, four faces, six edges and six bond angles.

blocks.prompt: 41 Why are CH₄, SiH₄ and CCl₄ tetrahedral?
blocks.explanation: Each central atom has four bond pairs and no lone pair (AB₄). The four pairs avoid repulsion by pointing to the corners of a regular tetrahedron, so each bond angle is 109.5°.

book_ref.quote: On the same grounds, SiH₄, GeH₄, CCl₄ possess the similar shape.

blocks.text: 3.3.3 Applications of the VSEPR model in drug designing

blocks.prompt: 42 Define drug, target and ligand.
blocks.explanation: Drug: a chemical substance that prevents, diagnoses or treats a disease. Target (substrate): the specific point or process in the body with which a drug interacts, e.g. enzymes, proteins, nucleic acids. Ligand: the bioactive molecule of the drug that binds to the target.

book_ref.quote: Drugs interact with human body at specific points, or with specific processes called targets or substrates

blocks.prompt: 43 Why is molecular shape important in drug design?
blocks.explanation: Only ligands with a suitable shape fit the active site of a biological target, as a specific key fits a specific lock. VSEPR helps find shapes for substrate recognition, ligand specificity and antibody recognition.

book_ref.quote: Molecular shape is an important feature that determines how a drug interacts with a biological target.

blocks.prompt: 44 How does aspirin relieve pain?
blocks.explanation: Aspirin binds to the active site of the enzyme COX (cyclooxygenase) through its acetyl group (–OCCH₃). The shapes of the COX active site and the acetyl group are compatible, so binding succeeds and blocks COX, which causes pain.

book_ref.quote: Therefore, the binding is successful to block COX, which is a cause of the pain in the body.

blocks.prompt: 45 State any three postulates of valence bond theory.
blocks.explanation: (1) A covalent bond forms when half-filled valence orbitals of two atoms with similar energy overlap. (2) Greater overlap gives a stronger bond. (3) Covalent bonds are directional; the direction depends on the shape and mode of the overlapping orbitals.

book_ref.quote: VBT is concerned with both the formation of bonds and the shapes of molecules.

blocks.prompt: 46 Why is VBT considered better than the VSEPR model?
blocks.explanation: VSEPR predicts and explains shapes of molecules but gives no reason for bond formation. VBT explains both the formation of bonds (by overlap of half-filled orbitals) and the shapes of molecules.

book_ref.quote: This method of describing a covalent bond considers a molecule as a combination of atoms.

blocks.prompt: 47 What is a sigma bond? Name the types of overlap that form it, with one example each.
blocks.explanation: A sigma bond forms by linear (head-on) overlap of two half-filled orbitals on adjacent atoms along the nuclear axis. s-s overlap: H₂; s-p overlap: HCl; p-p overlap: Cl₂.

book_ref.quote: Both s and p orbitals can overlap head-on to form sigma bonds.

blocks.prompt: 48 Why is the electron density in H₂ symmetrical while that in HCl is not?
blocks.explanation: In H₂ two identical H atoms overlap their s orbitals, so the paired electrons are symmetrical around the two nuclei. In HCl the s orbital of H overlaps the p orbital of Cl; Cl is more electronegative, so the density is higher near Cl and HCl is polar.

book_ref.quote: After the bond formation, the electrons are paired up and the electron density in this molecule is symmetrical

blocks.prompt: 49 How is the H₂S molecule formed according to VBT? What is its bond angle?
blocks.explanation: Two half-filled 3p orbitals of S (3py and 3pz) overlap with the 1s orbitals of two H atoms, giving two σ bonds. The molecule is v-shaped with a bond angle of 92°.

book_ref.quote: The two 3p (say 3py and 3pz) orbitals of sulfur containing one electron each

blocks.prompt: 50 Why is the bond angle in H₂S (92°) smaller than in H₂O (104.5°)?
blocks.explanation: According to the chapter, the orbitals of S are larger and the lone pair exerts a stronger repulsion on the bond pairs, so the H–S–H angle is compressed to 92°.

book_ref.quote: The bond angle in H₂O is 104.5°, whereas in H₂S, it is 92°.

blocks.prompt: 51 In O₂, why do the py orbitals form a π bond and not a σ bond?
blocks.explanation: After the px orbitals overlap end-to-end on the nuclear axis (σ bond), the py orbitals of the two atoms are parallel to each other. They can only overlap sideways, with lobes above and below the plane of the nuclei, which gives a π bond.

book_ref.quote: However, the py orbitals on both atoms are aligned parallel to each other.

blocks.text: 3.5 Atomic orbital hybridization and shapes of molecules

blocks.prompt: 52 Define hybridization. State two conditions for it.
blocks.explanation: Hybridization is the mixing of atomic orbitals of slightly different energies and shapes to form a new set of equivalent orbitals of the same energy and shape. Conditions: it occurs in a single atom (or ion), and only orbitals of comparable energies mix.

book_ref.quote: A process in which atomic orbitals of slightly different energies and shapes are mixed together

blocks.prompt: 53 How many hybrid orbitals are formed in sp, sp² and sp³ hybridization? Give the rule.
blocks.explanation: The number of mixing orbitals always equals the number of hybrid orbitals. sp: 1 + 1 = 2; sp²: 1 + 2 = 3; sp³: 1 + 3 = 4.

book_ref.quote: The number of mixing orbitals is always equal to the number of the resulting hybrid orbitals.

blocks.prompt: 54 How is methane formed by sp³ hybridization?
blocks.explanation: In carbon one 2s and three 2p orbitals (excited state) mix to give four equal sp³ hybrid orbitals arranged tetrahedrally. Each overlaps with the 1s orbital of an H atom, giving four sp³-s σ bonds directed to the corners of a regular tetrahedron (109.5°).

book_ref.quote: The four new hybrid orbitals of equal energy have a tetrahedral geometry with carbon nucleus at the center.

blocks.prompt: 55 Describe the shape of an sp³ hybrid orbital.
blocks.explanation: Each sp³ hybrid orbital has two lobes, one larger and one smaller. For simplicity the smaller lobe is usually not shown when the four sp³ orbitals are drawn together.

book_ref.quote: For the sake of simplicity, the smaller lobe is usually not shown

blocks.prompt: 56 Explain sp² hybridization in BF₃.
blocks.explanation: In excited B, one 2s and two 2p orbitals mix to give three half-filled sp² orbitals at 120° in a plane. Each overlaps with a half-filled 2pz orbital of F, so BF₃ is triangular planar with 120° angles.

book_ref.quote: The three outermost orbitals of B mix together to give three sp² hybrid orbitals.

blocks.prompt: 57 Explain sp hybridization in BeCl₂.
blocks.explanation: In excited Be, one 2s and one 2p orbital mix to give two equal sp hybrid orbitals at 180°. Each overlaps with a half-filled p orbital of Cl, so BeCl₂ is linear.

book_ref.quote: The sp hybridization explains the geometry of linear molecules such as beryllium chloride

blocks.prompt: 58 Differentiate between sp² and sp³ hybridization.
blocks.explanation: sp² mixes one s and two p orbitals; sp³ mixes one s and three p orbitals.

book_ref.quote: In sp² hybridization, one s and two p atomic orbitals of an atom intermix to form three orbitals

rows: One s and two p orbitals mix.
One s and three p orbitals mix.
Three hybrid orbitals.
Four hybrid orbitals.
Trigonal planar, 120°.
Tetrahedral, 109.5°.
Example: BF₃.
Example: CH₄.

blocks.prompt: 59 What does a bond order of zero mean? Give an example from the chapter.
blocks.explanation: Bond order = (a − b)/2 is the number of bonds between two atoms. Zero means the bonding and anti-bonding electrons are equal, so no bond is formed and the molecule does not exist. Example: He₂, (2 − 2)/2 = 0.

book_ref.quote: The number of bonds formed between two atoms after the atomic orbitals overlap, is called the bond order

blocks.prompt: 60 Differentiate between bonding and anti-bonding molecular orbitals.
blocks.explanation: Bonding MOs come from same-sign overlap and are lower in energy; anti-bonding MOs come from opposite-sign overlap and are higher in energy.

book_ref.quote: When same sign orbitals overlap, the bonding molecular orbital

rows: Formed when orbitals of the same sign overlap.
Formed when orbitals of opposite signs overlap.
Lower energy than the parent atomic orbitals.
Higher energy than the parent atomic orbitals.
Symbol σ or π.
Symbol σ* or π*.
In H₂: symmetrical about the nuclear axis.
In H₂: electron density away from the nuclei.

blocks.prompt: 61 A diatomic species has 6 bonding and 4 anti-bonding electrons. Find its bond order.
blocks.explanation: Bond order = (a − b)/2 = (6 − 4)/2 = 1. The atoms are joined by one bond.

book_ref.quote: The molecular orbital approach explains the results of quantum mechanical calculations for covalent bonding.

blocks.prompt: 62 How are π molecular orbitals formed? Where is their electron density?
blocks.explanation: When py or pz orbitals with parallel axes interact sideways, π MOs form. The bonding π(2py) and π(2pz) have zero electron density on the nuclear axis (nodal plane); the anti-bonding π*(2py) and π*(2pz) have the least density in the inter-nuclear region.

book_ref.quote: anti-bonding molecular orbitals π*(2py) and π*(2pz) have the least electron density in the inter-nuclear region

blocks.prompt: 63 Differentiate between the head-on and sideways approach of p orbitals in MOT.
blocks.explanation: Head-on approach gives σ MOs; sideways approach gives π MOs.

book_ref.quote: Here, the p-orbitals of the two atoms approach along the same axis

rows: p orbitals approach along the same axis (x-axis).
Axes of the p orbitals (py or pz) are parallel.
Gives σ(2px) and σ*(2px) MOs.
Gives π(2py), π(2pz) and π*(2py), π*(2pz) MOs.

blocks.text: 3.6.1 Molecular orbital diagrams of some diatomic molecules and their bond orders

blocks.prompt: 64 Why does He₂ not exist according to MOT?
blocks.explanation: Two He atoms (1s²) give 4 electrons: two in σ1s and two in σ*1s. Bond order = (2 − 2)/2 = 0. With zero bond order no bond forms, so He₂ is not formed.

book_ref.quote: Out of four electrons, two enter the bonding molecular orbital

blocks.prompt: 65 Relate the bond orders of N₂ and O₂ to their bond energies in Table 3.2.
blocks.explanation: N₂: bond order (6 − 0)/2 = 3 (N≡N), bond energy 941 kJ mol⁻¹. O₂: bond order (6 − 2)/2 = 2 (O=O), bond energy 495 kJ mol⁻¹. The higher bond order of N₂ goes with its much higher bond energy, as multiple bonds are stronger.

book_ref.quote: Therefore, there are three covalent bonds between the nitrogen atoms in this molecule.

blocks.prompt: 66 What are paramagnetic substances? Why is O₂ paramagnetic?
blocks.explanation: Paramagnetic substances are attracted by a magnetic field; they have one or more unpaired electrons. The MO diagram of O₂ shows two unpaired electrons, one each in π*(2py) and π*(2pz), giving O₂ a net magnetic field.

book_ref.quote: Paramagnetic substances have one or more unpaired electrons in them.

blocks.prompt: 67 Calculate the bond order of O₂ and state what it shows.
blocks.explanation: From the 2p molecular orbitals: bonding electrons 6, anti-bonding electrons 2. Bond order = (6 − 2)/2 = 2: one σ and one π bond, i.e. O=O double bond.

book_ref.quote: The bond order of oxygen is 2

blocks.prompt: 68 Differentiate between the energy order of the 2p molecular orbitals in N₂ and O₂.
blocks.explanation: The position of σ2px relative to the π2p orbitals differs.

book_ref.quote: whereas, 2p orbitals give six molecular orbitals which are arranged in the increasing order of energy as

rows: π2py = π2pz lie below σ2px.
σ2px lies below π2py = π2pz.
σ2s < σ*2s < π2py = π2pz < σ2px < π*2py = π*2pz < σ*2px
σ2s < σ*2s < σ2px < π2py = π2pz < π*2py = π*2pz < σ*2px

blocks.prompt: 69 Why does liquid oxygen get suspended between the poles of a strong magnet?
blocks.explanation: O₂ has two unpaired electrons (in π*2py and π*2pz), so it has a net magnetic field that interacts with the external field. Being paramagnetic, liquid O₂ is attracted and held between the poles.

book_ref.quote: Due to the presence of these unpaired electrons, oxygen molecule has a net magnetic field

blocks.prompt: 70 What are van der Waals forces? Name their three types.
blocks.explanation: Van der Waals (intermolecular) forces are weak attractions between all kinds of atoms and molecules when they are sufficiently close; they bring molecules together and give physical properties. Types: (1) London dispersion (instantaneous dipole-induced dipole) forces, (2) permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces, (3) hydrogen bonding.

book_ref.quote: These forces are believed to exist between all kinds of atoms and molecules when they are sufficiently close

blocks.prompt: 71 Define bond energy. How is it determined and what is its unit?
blocks.explanation: Bond energy is the average energy required to break all bonds of a particular type in one mole of a substance. It is determined experimentally by measuring the heat involved in a chemical reaction; unit kJ mol⁻¹.

book_ref.quote: It is determined experimentally by measuring the heat involved in a chemical reaction

blocks.prompt: 72 Why is the bond energy of H–F (565 kJ mol⁻¹) greater than that of H–I (295 kJ mol⁻¹)?
blocks.explanation: The electronegativity difference between H and F is much larger than between H and I. Greater difference means greater bond polarity, which gives additional attractive force between the atoms, so H–F is stronger (by 565 − 295 = 270 kJ mol⁻¹).

book_ref.quote: The data show that the bond energy of a bond rises with the increasing electronegativity difference

blocks.prompt: 73 Using Table 3.2, find the energy needed to break all H–Cl bonds in 3 mol of HCl.
blocks.explanation: H–Cl bond energy = 427 kJ mol⁻¹. Energy = 3 mol × 427 kJ mol⁻¹ = 1281 kJ.

book_ref.quote: Look at the bond energies of H-X type of compounds, where X=F, Cl, Br, I.

blocks.prompt: 74 Name the factors on which the strength (bond energy) of a bond depends.
blocks.explanation: (1) Electronegativity difference of the bonded atoms: greater difference, higher bond energy. (2) Size of the atoms. Also, multiple bonds are stronger than single bonds: C≡C (839) > C=C (614) > C–C (347) kJ mol⁻¹.

book_ref.quote: Electronegativity difference of bonded atoms

blocks.prompt: 75 Define bond length. Name the techniques used to find it.
blocks.explanation: Bond length is the distance between the nuclei of two atoms forming a covalent bond. It is found experimentally by electron diffraction, X-ray diffraction or spectral studies.

book_ref.quote: Bond length is the distance between the nuclei of two atoms forming a covalent bond.

blocks.prompt: 76 Why is the C–Cl bond (180 pm) longer than the C–F bond (135 pm)?
blocks.explanation: Bond length increases with the size of the atoms. The Cl atom is much larger than F, so the C–Cl bond is longer (180 − 135 = 45 pm).

book_ref.quote: This is because the Cl atom is much larger.

blocks.prompt: 77 The Si–F bond in SiF₄ is about 155 pm, while covalent radii (Si = 117 pm, F = 64 pm) predict 181 pm. Find the shortening and give its reason.
blocks.explanation: Expected = 117 + 64 = 181 pm; shortening = 181 − 155 = 26 pm (about 14%). The large electronegativity difference gives the bond ionic character, whose additional attraction shortens the bond.

book_ref.quote: With the rise in electronegativity difference between the bonded atoms, the bond becomes shortened.

blocks.prompt: 78 Compare bond energy and bond length of C–C, C=C and C≡C using Tables 3.2 and 3.3.
blocks.explanation: Bond energy rises and bond length falls from single to triple bond: C–C 347 kJ mol⁻¹, 154 pm; C=C 614 kJ mol⁻¹, 133 pm; C≡C 839 kJ mol⁻¹, 120 pm. The triple bond is the strongest and shortest.

book_ref.quote: The bond lengths are experimentally determined by physical techniques

blocks.prompt: 79 Differentiate between bond energy and bond length.
blocks.explanation: Bond energy is an energy; bond length is a distance.

book_ref.quote: Bond energy is a measure of the strength of a bond and its reactivity.

blocks.text: 3.10 A comparison among ionic, covalent, metallic bonds and intermolecular forces

blocks.prompt: 80 Why are ionic, covalent and metallic bonds termed true chemical bonds?
blocks.explanation: Because they affect the chemical properties of a substance: they form new species through transfer and sharing of electrons. Intermolecular forces only bring molecules closer and influence physical properties.

book_ref.quote: Chemical bonds, i.e. ionic, covalent, and metallic bond are usually termed as true chemical bonds

blocks.prompt: 81 Differentiate between chemical bonds and intermolecular forces.
blocks.explanation: Chemical bonds form new species and are strong; intermolecular forces act between molecules and are weak.

book_ref.quote: It also reveals that chemical bonds are generally much stronger than intermolecular forces.

rows: Form new species through transfer and sharing of electrons.
Bring molecules closer together.
Affect chemical properties.
Influence physical properties.
Strong: NaCl ionic 760, O–H 464 kJ mol⁻¹.
Weak: hydrogen bonding 20-50, van der Waals 1-20 kJ mol⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: 82 Why is the metallic bond weaker than ionic and covalent bonds?
blocks.explanation: Its average bond energy is only 100-150 kJ mol⁻¹. A satisfactory argument for this low strength is the extensive delocalization of electrons within the metallic crystal.

book_ref.quote: In any case, the metallic bond is weaker than both the ionic and covalent bonds.

blocks.prompt: 83 Arrange the following in decreasing order of strength using Table 3.4: hydrogen bonding, ionic bond in NaCl, van der Waals forces, O–H bond in water.
blocks.explanation: Ionic bond in NaCl (760) > O–H bond in water (464) > hydrogen bonding (20-50) > van der Waals forces (1-20 kJ mol⁻¹).

book_ref.quote: Table 3.4 provides a comparison among different chemical bonds and intermolecular forces.
